stops.accessibility: Flat paved park paths, step free at the teahouse terrace; tables are close together and the morning crowd is thick.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Park entry is free. Tea is charged per gaiwan at the teahouse counter, roughly ¥20 at last check; ear-cleaning and shoe-shines are extras. Verify prices locally.
stops.insiderTip: Order jasmine tea and nurse one gaiwan all morning: the waiters refill it endlessly from metre-long-spout kettles without you asking.
stops.name: People's Park and Heming Teahouse
stops.narration:
Find a bamboo chair on the terrace, sit down, and listen. The click-clack around you is mahjong — a four-player tile game China plays the way other countries play cards — mixed with kettle hiss, gossip and somebody's caged thrush. You are inside Chengdu's living room.

This is People's Park, laid out in 1911 as one of the city's first public parks, and Heming Teahouse, pouring since 1923. A gaiwan is the lidded bowl-cup in front of you: leaves at the bottom, lid to hold them back while you sip. Tea costs on the order of ¥20 — the RMB, or renminbi, is China's currency, yuan the unit — and verify at the counter, because prices move. What you are really buying is the chair. Nobody here checks a watch. Retired men play marathon mahjong, couples share sunflower seeds, and the ear-cleaners work the rows: pay a small fee and a specialist scrapes your ears with thin steel picks and a tuning-fork tingle. It looks alarming and feels, devotees insist, wonderful.

Here is the mechanism worth carrying all day. Chengdu sits on a flat, irrigated plain that has fed it for two thousand years, and the local answer to abundance was never hurry — it was this. Outsiders call Chengdu lazy; Chengdu calls it living. The teahouse is not a break from the economy. It is the economy of attention, and you just bought in for the price of tea.

Finish your cup, keep the leaves for refills, and walk out of the park's west side. The Taoist palace is about 2.4 km west — roughly thirty-five minutes on foot, the longest stroll of the morning, all flat.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the park by the west side and head west along the grid for about 2.4 km — roughly thirty-five minutes on foot, all flat city pavement. The upturned eaves and yellow walls ahead are Qingyang Palace; enter through the main gate.
stops.openingHours: Park open daily, roughly 06:00 to 22:00. Heming pours from mid-morning; arrive before 10:00 for the full bustle.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Daderot, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.accessibility: Level courtyards with thresholds at hall doors; incense smoke is thick in the main court. Not fully step free.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Ticketed temple courtyard, about ¥10 at last check. Verify at the gate; prices and hours shift.
stops.insiderTip: Find the two bronze goats in the main hall's side court: one is a puzzle animal stitched from all twelve zodiac signs, and finding the mouse ears keeps children busy for ages.
stops.name: Qingyang Palace
stops.narration:
Step through the gate and the traffic falls away into pine shade and incense. You have left the mahjong behind and entered China's home-grown religion.

Qingyang — Green Ram Palace — is Chengdu's great Taoist temple. Taoism is the native Chinese teaching of the Way: the philosopher Laozi, the Old Master of the 500s BCE, traditionally credited with the Daodejing, the short strange book about yielding, softness and water wearing down stone. Monks here belong to the Quanzhen order, the orthodox school that runs major temples. The halls you see are mostly Qing rebuilding — the Qing being the dynasty, ruled by Manchu emperors from the north-east, that governed China from 1644 to 1912 — around older bones: the Eight Trigrams Pavilion with its octagonal roof, the bronze goat pair, the quiet reading courts.

Do the small ritual everyone does. Hold three sticks of incense, bow three times to each direction, and plant them in the burner. Nobody checks your beliefs. Then find the bronze goats: legend says Laozi appeared riding a green ox, and one goat here is a composite of all twelve zodiac animals, mouse ears to horse hooves. Rub the part of yourself that aches; the bronze shines where millions of hands agreed.

Ticket about ¥10, verify at the gate. And note the lesson for the next stop: this Taoist palace and the Buddhist monastery ahead have shared one city for centuries without fuss. Chengdu collects faiths the way it collects teas.

Now the honest part: Wenshu Monastery is 4.6 km north-east — roughly seventy minutes on foot along busy roads — so do not stroll it. Take the metro with a change or a taxi; allow about thirty minutes door to door.
stops.nextStopDirections: This is a hop, not a walk: Wenshu Monastery is 4.6 km north-east — roughly seventy minutes on foot along busy roads — so do not stroll it. Take the metro with one change or a taxi (about thirty minutes door to door) to Wenshu Monastery station, then walk a few minutes to the temple gate.
stops.openingHours: Open daily, roughly 08:00 to 18:00. Mornings are quietest; verify hours at the gate.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Daderot, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.accessibility: Mostly level courtyards with steps into the main halls; the vegetarian restaurant has stairs. Incense and crowds at midday.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free entry to the temple courtyards. The vegetarian restaurant and tea garden charge separately; verify locally.
stops.insiderTip: Eat lunch at the monastery's vegetarian restaurant behind the halls: mock-duck and mapo tofu with no meat, and the queue of locals is the review.
stops.name: Wenshu Monastery
stops.narration:
You arrive to chanting and the sweet smoke of a hundred incense coils. This is the Buddhist half of Chengdu's double faith, and it sounds different from the palace you just left.

Wenshu Monastery is named for Wenshu — Manjushri, the bodhisattva of wisdom. Buddhism came to China from India around two thousand years ago; a bodhisattva is an enlightened being who stays behind to help everyone else get free. This is a Chan temple — Chan being the Chinese meditation school the Japanese call Zen — first raised in the Tang dynasty of the 600s to 900s and rebuilt in its present form under the Qing emperor Kangxi around 1700, after the wars that ended the Ming left it in ruins. Entry is free, though the restaurant and tea garden charge.

Walk the five halls in order and watch the statues get sterner as you go: guardian kings at the gate, the laughing Buddha-to-be, Buddhas of past, present and future. Lay people read fortunes, buy strings of beads, and drink tea in the garden behind the chanting. If it is lunchtime, join the queue at the vegetarian restaurant — Buddhist temples cook no meat, and this one is famous for it.

Hold the two stops together. A Taoist palace honouring Laozi and a Buddhist monastery honouring wisdom, four kilometres apart, both packed, neither threatened. That easy sharing is the city's real religion, and it is why the teahouses stay full.

Next is another ride: the Kuanzhai lanes are 3.0 km south-west — about forty-five minutes on foot — so take the metro with a change or a short taxi.
stops.nextStopDirections: This is a hop, not a walk: the Kuanzhai lanes are 3.0 km south-west — about forty-five minutes on foot along city roads — so ride. Take the metro with one change or a short taxi (about twenty minutes) to the Kuanzhai Alley area, then enter the lanes on foot.
stops.openingHours: Open daily, roughly 08:00 to 17:00. The vegetarian restaurant serves lunch until early afternoon; verify locally.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Daderot, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.accessibility: Paved lanes, mostly level but crowded; flagstones can be slick in December drizzle. Step free enough for slow wheels with help.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to stroll the public lanes. Shops, snacks, courtyard houses and performances charge separately; verify prices as you go.
stops.insiderTip: Walk all three lanes end to end before buying anything: Wide Alley for show, Narrow Alley for food, Well Alley for the quiet old walls — then spend once.
stops.name: Kuanzhai Alleys
stops.narration:
Three grey-brick lanes run parallel in front of you, and their names are the whole story. Kuan means wide, zhai means narrow: Wide Alley, Narrow Alley, and the quiet Well Alley behind them.

These lanes are what is left of the Lesser City, the walled garrison where Manchu bannermen — soldiers of the north-eastern people whose emperors ruled Qing China from 1644 to 1912 — were stationed to watch over Chengdu. Courtyard houses with deep eaves, spirit screens behind the doors, wells shared by neighbours. In 2008 the city rebuilt the district as a heritage street: grey brick outside, boutiques and snack stalls inside. Supporters call it rescue; critics call it a stage set with the plumbing moved. Say both in one breath and keep walking, because both are partly true — the walls are new-ish, the lane pattern is real, and the crowds are gloriously unbothered by the debate.

Graze as you go. Narrow Alley is the food lane: rabbit heads, dan-dan noodles, sugar-oil fruit, all cheap, all cashless — China pays by phone, though cash in RMB still works. Peek into the open courtyards for shadow-puppet stalls and opera singers rehearsing behind glass. The lanes themselves are free; everything edible costs, so verify as you go.

When you have grazed enough, walk south about a kilometre — fifteen minutes, flat — down to the Culture Park teahouse where the opera plays.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the lanes at the south end and walk south about one kilometre — roughly fifteen minutes, flat pavements — toward the Culture Park and Qintai Road. The Sichuan opera teahouse is signposted there; book at the door.
stops.openingHours: Lanes are open access all day. Shops roughly 09:00 to 22:00; evenings are liveliest.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Daderot, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.accessibility: Theatre seating with steps to most rows; ask staff for an aisle seat. Show is loud — sudden fire and cymbals.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Ticketed evening performance, roughly ¥100–200 depending on seat and tea at last check. Verify times and prices at the door; shows sell out on weekends.
stops.insiderTip: Sit in the first few rows and watch the sleeves, not the faces: the masks change under cover of a fan-flick or a sleeve-snap, and closeness ruins the magic beautifully.
stops.name: Shufeng Yayun Opera Teahouse
stops.narration:
Take your seat, pour the tea that comes with the ticket, and wait for the man in the embroidered robe. What happens next is the fastest secret in China.

This is Sichuan opera, chuanju, performed nightly in this Culture Park teahouse with the audience at tables the way opera was always meant to be drunk. Its famous trick is bianlian — face-changing: the performer swaps painted masks in a fraction of a second, ten, twenty masks in one scene, each new face snapping on with a fan-flick, a sleeve-snap, a turn of the head. The method is a trade secret passed master to disciple, and the state lists it as protected heritage. Watch for the companion trick too: spitting fire, a mouthful of oil breathed across a torch into a plume.

Tickets run on the order of ¥100 to ¥200 with tea — verify at the door, and check show times, because they shift by season and sell out on weekends. If you cannot stay for the evening show, the matinee or the museum corners still teach the mechanism: opera here was never a palace art. It was teahouse entertainment for people exactly like the ones you sat with this morning.

Two faiths, three lanes, one opera — and one kingdom left. Ride south to the shrine of the strategist: 2.6 km, about forty minutes on foot, so take the metro or a taxi.
stops.nextStopDirections: This is the last hop: the Wuhou Shrine is 2.6 km south — about forty minutes on foot — so take the metro or a taxi (about twenty-five minutes) to the Wuhou Shrine area, then enter through the main gate on Wuhouci Street.
stops.openingHours: Shows most evenings; daytime teahouse and exhibits in the afternoon. Check times at the door on the day.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Zoharby, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.accessibility: Walled park with level main paths and steps into each hall; the tomb mound path is stepped. Bluntly: a slow walk with stairs at every pavilion.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Ticketed temple park, about ¥50 at last check. Verify at the gate; last entry is well before closing.
stops.insiderTip: Read the stone couplets in the main hall before the statues: the famous Tang-dynasty inscription praising Zhuge Liang is still the sharpest character sketch in the park.
stops.name: Wuhou Shrine
stops.narration:
You enter through old cypress shade into the kingdom this whole walk was named for. Shu is not just a brand here. It was a state.

Wuhou Shrine honours Zhuge Liang, the strategist-chancellor of Shu Han — one of the Three Kingdoms that split China from 220 to 280 after the Han dynasty fell — alongside his king Liu Bei, whose tomb mound rises inside these same walls. The halls are Qing rebuilding around a much older cult: rulers and rebels have paid court to Zhuge Liang for 1,600 years. His statue, the stern one holding the feather fan, gets the incense; Liu Bei's gets the flowers.

Now the twist the park teaches honestly. Half of what China 'knows' about these men comes not from chronicles but from the Romance of the Three Kingdoms, the rip-roaring 1300s novel that turned a failed kingdom into the tragedy everyone weeps at. The novel made Shu the good guys: loyal, clever, doomed. Chengdu has been dining on that story ever since — note the opera masks you just saw, the snacks named for generals, the panda named after nobody at all. History happened; the novel decided what it meant. Both are on sale in the gift shop.

Ticket about ¥50, verify at the gate, last entry well before closing. Then step out of the side gate: the lanterns are already lit next door, and dinner is a 250-metre walk.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave by the side gate onto the old street and walk about 250 metres — a few minutes — into the lantern-lit lanes of Jinli. Go hungry and keep the evening short.
stops.openingHours: Open daily, roughly 08:00 to 18:00. Last entry well before closing; verify at the gate.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Daderot, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.accessibility: Flagstoned lanes, level but jammed shoulder-to-shoulder after dark; pickpockets work the crush. Not a calm roll for wheels.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to stroll. Food, crafts and bars charge separately and run tourist prices; verify as you go and keep cashless payment or small RMB notes ready.
stops.insiderTip: Eat savoury first, sweet last, and leave by the far end: the stalls thin out past the stage square, and the exit drops you near taxis back to the centre.
stops.name: Jinli Old Street (Evening)
stops.narration:
You step into lantern light and the smell of chilli and sugar, and the day's quiet ends on purpose. This is Jinli after dark.

Jinli — brocade lane — is named for the Shu brocade, the patterned silk whose workshops made this kingdom rich two thousand years ago. Today's street is a Qing-style rebuild from the early 2000s:_base tea taverns, puppet stages, sugar painters, rabbit heads and stinky tofu by the dozen. It is commercial, crowded, and completely sincere about being commercial. Ninety minutes is the dose: long enough to graze the full lane, short enough to beat the crush, the inflated prices and the pickpockets that come with fame. Eat savoury first and sweet last, keep your phone zipped, and assume every queue is either very good or very photographed.

Then stand still a moment under the lanterns and collect the day. A teahouse chair this morning, a Taoist goat, a Buddhist chant, three lanes of brick, a mask that changed faster than your eyes, a strategist's tomb — and underneath it all the plain that paid for everything, still growing rice in the grey. Chengdu's ease is not an accident. It is irrigation, faith, story and spice, compounded over two millennia.

End of the walk. Take a taxi back to the centre, order hotpot — mala broth, the numbing-spicy mix of chilli and Sichuan pepper — and sleep late. The pandas and the Sanxingdui bronzes are separate day trips, and they can wait.
stops.nextStopDirections: End of the walk. Retrace the lane to either end for taxis; the ride back to the city centre takes about twenty minutes in evening traffic. Keep belongings zipped in the crowd.
stops.openingHours: Lanes open access daily into the late evening; stalls roughly 09:00 to 22:00. Come after dark for the lanterns.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Zairon, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start around 09:00 so the teahouse is roaring and temples are open; ride between clusters through the middle of the day and reach Jinli after dark. December to February suits this walk: cold but made for teahouses.
tour.difficulty: Easy on the feet, honest on the map: about 3.6 km of flat strolling plus three metro/taxi hops. Walked end to end the route is 13.7 km and about three and a half hours on foot — do not.
tour.imageCredits: Photographs are bundled from Wikimedia Commons under public domain or Creative Commons licences. Individual credits appear under each stop's photograph.
tour.overviewText:
You hear Chengdu before you see it: the click of mahjong tiles under plane trees, kettle steam curling over a hundred lidded cups, somebody's grandfather clearing his throat like a chairman. Sit down. You live here now.

Chengdu is the capital of Shu, the low green basin of the Sichuan plain, and its ease is engineered. Two thousand years ago the engineer Li Bing tamed the Min River with Dujiangyan — a waterworks that splits the current without a dam and still irrigates the plain today — and the plain has been called the Land of Abundance ever since. Flat land, full granaries, soft rain: a city that never had to hurry, so it never learned how. Twenty million people now live in the sprawl, but the old centre still keeps office hours around the teahouse.

Daily life here runs on tea and tiles. A gaiwan is a lidded bowl-cup you sip through half-closed; mahjong is the four-player tile game whose click is the city's percussion. Retirees play for stakes of pride, office workers sneak afternoon sessions, and nobody apologises. The faiths share the pavement the same way: Qingyang Palace honours Laozi, the Old Master of Taoism, China's native teaching of yielding and the Way, while Wenshu Monastery chants to the Buddhist ideal of wisdom a few kilometres away — Taoist and Buddhist, incense and chanting, no walls between them. What pays for the leisure is partly the panda: the giant bear of the Sichuan mountains is on every logo, and the breeding research base north of town draws the crowds that fill the hotels. In December you will want the other subsidy: hotpot, the boiling mala broth — numbing-spicy with Sichuan pepper and chilli — that winter was invented for. Plan at least three.

The walk starts in a People's Park teahouse, crosses the old city to a Taoist palace and a Buddhist monastery, then rides south through Qing-dynasty lanes and an opera teahouse to a strategist's shrine and lantern-lit Jinli after dark. The panda base and the Sanxingdui bronzes are separate day trips — Chengdu's headline acts, but not this walk.

December practicals: the basin traps grey cloud and damp cold around 5 to 10 degrees, so layer up and treat teahouses as warming stations. Fees are in RMB, the renminbi (yuan the unit), and every price and hour below needs verifying at the gate — they move. Three legs of this route are metro or taxi hops, stated honestly against their on-foot numbers; the lanes themselves are flat but crowded and slick with drizzle.

Come thirsty. Chengdu rewards sitters, and your chair has been waiting since 1923.
tour.summary: Teahouses, temples and lantern light: a day across old Chengdu from a People's Park gaiwan to Qingyang and Wenshu, the Qing lanes, Sichuan opera and an evening finish in Jinli — with three honest metro hops.
tour.title: Chengdu – Teahouses & Alleys
